claims.text: The baseline TiVNbTa alloy is a single-phase BCC dendritic material.
Baseline TiVNbTa has a yield strength of approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
Baseline TiVNbTa has a compressive strength of approximately 423 MPa at 1273 K and 30% strain.
Adding approximately 5 at.% W to TiVNbTa will improve high-temperature strength retention.
The approximately 5 at.% W addition will maintain adequate ductility.
The approximately 5 at.% W addition will maintain adequate thermal conductivity for heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
Added W atoms will dissolve in the BCC TiVNbTa matrix.
Dissolved W will increase lattice distortion and produce solid-solution strengthening.
The W addition may produce nanoscale precipitates that impede dislocation motion.
W addition will retard thermally activated dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding.
Retarding dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will reduce high-temperature softening and increase strength.
The modified alloy will retain a single-phase structure.
Retaining a single-phase structure will support sufficient ductility and effective heat transfer.
At 1273 K, the W-modified alloy will have at least 20% greater yield strength than the approximately 330 MPa baseline.
At 1273 K, the W-modified alloy will retain ductility of approximately 30% strain or greater.
The predicted enhancement applies at temperatures up to 1273 K and strains up to 30%.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure or higher strain rates may cause phase instability or embrittlement.
Brittle precipitates formed during extended high-temperature exposure could impair ductility or heat-transfer efficiency.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator allows nanoscale precipitate formation as part of the strengthening explanation, whereas the mechanism simultaneously attributes retained ductility and heat transfer to retention of a single-phase structure. Actual precipitates would ordinarily constitute an additional phase unless they are merely clusters or another qualification is supplied.
